blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.
blocks.zh: 每个多模式-LLM多选择基准都以打分规则为结尾,将一个模型的反应,往往是自由形式的文本而不是干净的选项字母,转换成右/错的判决,埋入其代码. 与数据集不同的是,这一规则是在没有正当理由的情况下选择的,并且没有经过审查,然而它却设置了已公布的数字. 我们转载了五个开放式视觉语言模型(VLMs)的8个经同行评审的基准的官方分数,该分数符合单一的16GB GPU,并引入了被盲目的人-+-LLM法官裁决(Cohen's kappa=0.956),恢复了模型实际回答的内容. 单打分规则在相同输出上移动了最多22分的精度,然而,只要一个模型释放出干净的选项字母,则精确的为0分,所以它会隐藏在强模长板上. 造成破坏的是倒行逆施而不是胡言乱语:我们衡量的不遵守情况最高的基准有一个完全为零的产物,因为它的得分者没有猜测,而是投弃权票;不遵守0.000的推理模型仍然摇摆着9.5分,与它所保持的痕迹成正比。 没有标准规则是可靠的:对它最接近的选项入分的答案进行不回答,但从未给过正确答案,弃权者丢弃了用文字表达的答案,而概率分数跟随了答题前题,所以一个单等积分就能用运气来拼凑能力,而不是测量。 我们公布所有代码,标签,协议, 并论证基准应该报告不遵守率和至少两个规则, 而不是一个未经审查的等级。

blocks.en:
Consider a vision-language model asked whether an industrial part is defective, with options “(A) Yes”
and “(B) No.” It replies: “The object is a nail.” The model never answered the question. Yet
MMAD [ 15 ] , an ICLR’25 benchmark, scores this response correct : its grader calls difflib.get_close_matches(response, options, cutoff=0.0) , which with a zero threshold snaps
any string to the lexically nearest option: here “Yes,” by character overlap, not base rate. An abstaining grader scores
the same response wrong . A likelihood grader returns whatever the model’s logits prefer. A human
reading it records that the model gave no answer . Four graders, four verdicts, one output
(Fig. 1 ). The grade came from the grader, not the model.

blocks.en:
This is not a quirk of one benchmark. Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark must decide what to do when a
model’s free-form text does not cleanly name an option, and that decision, a few lines at the bottom
of a scoring script, is made differently across the field: a no-threshold snap (MMAD [ 15 ] ,
OmniMedVQA [ 14 ] , PMC-VQA [ 36 ] ), a random fallback (MMMU [ 33 ] ,
ScienceQA [ 20 ] ), a default class (POPE [ 18 ] ), abstention, or likelihood scoring. These
benchmarks cleared top-tier peer review and are cited widely, but reviewers judged the datasets ;
the grader was an unexamined implementation detail that produced numbers which looked reasonable, so
it went unopened. This paper opens it.

blocks.en:
“Just parse the letter and mark the rest wrong” (abstention) is one choice among several, and it is not
obviously right: a model that answers “No.” in words, or reasons correctly and is then cut off before
emitting a letter, is marked wrong. Conversely, the no-threshold snap rewards rambles that never commit.
The rules are not interchangeable, and which one a benchmark ships changes its leaderboard. We scope
this audit to the locally deployable regime (open models of ≤ 13 {\leq}13 B on one consumer GPU),
the binding constraint for the applications these benchmarks target: privacy-bound medical VQA and
air-gapped industrial inspection, where a frontier API model is not an option. Where a model emits clean letters the rules
coincide, so the choice is invisible there; in the regime practitioners are confined to, the scores
that guide deployment inherit it.

blocks.en:
A line of work studies the format sensitivity of multimodal-LLM scoring: first-token logits versus
decoded text on answers the model did give in parseable form [ 23 , 37 ] , and
whether models should be allowed to abstain on unanswerable inputs [ 24 ] . Standardized harnesses do
not dissolve the problem: VLMEvalKit [ 9 ] , which powers the OpenVLM leaderboard, falls back
to random.choice once its extraction retries fail and to a fixed sentinel under its parse-only
policy: the two idioms we audit, shipped as defaults. The closest prior work
anchors answer extraction to human judgment for text LLMs and does annotate non-answers,
refusals and truncation among them [ 25 , App. A.3] ; what it does not do is grade them, recording a miss instead, and it varies prompt format at a fixed extractor rather
than the scorer at fixed outputs. We audit what the released scorer credits when no answer is extractable, a different contrast, and find 21 21 – 22 22 points. The reason ours can be this
large is mechanical. Text LLMs mostly emit a parseable letter; on the open VLMs
practitioners can actually deploy, the fallback fires on 29 29 – 37 % 37\% of items. Multimodal is where the
fallback stops being a rounding error and starts setting the number, which is why this audit had to be
done here, in the spirit of evaluation reality-checks in other
subfields [ 22 , 26 ] .

That the parse-failure rule varies and is unreported across the
field is a code audit of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks (Table 1 ), six of which
manufacture a verdict and two of which do not. That no rule reliably recovers what the model
answered is a stronger claim, demonstrated where we have human ground truth: binary MMAD and four-option
medical PMC-VQA. We anchor it on binary MMAD by design, not by limitation: yes/no is where blinded
readers agree almost perfectly on what a model said (inter-annotator κ = 0.91 \kappa=0.91 ), so it is where the
grader’s fabrication is certifiable rather than asserted. Breadth is carried by the field-wide
survey, proof by the binary anchor.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Lyu et al. [23] report large disagreements between a model’s first-token logit and its decoded
free-text answer on multiple-choice questions; others study option-order and prompt robustness and the
generative-versus-discriminative gap [ 37 ] ; Rosenthal et al. [27] further show that
semantically-neutral prompt-format changes alone reorder MLLM leaderboards, as does prompt format in text
LLMs [ 28 ] ; Alzahrani et al. [2] perturb the benchmark and the
answer-selection method together and move leaderboard rank by up to eight positions. All vary the input , or analyze answers produced in parseable form. We hold the outputs byte-identical and
vary only the parse- failure rule, anchoring each to an external human label rather than to another
automated rule.

blocks.en:
A parallel line improves how a parseable answer is recovered or standardized: trained extractors
that pinpoint the option a model chose [ 32 ] , standardized prompt-and-parse protocols [ 12 ] ,
reproducibility practices for evaluation harnesses [ 6 ] , and, for text LLMs, evidence that
answer-extraction choices disagree with human judgment on MCQA [ 25 ] , and that
the extraction algorithm alone shifts reasoning-model results [ 16 ] ; in the
multimodal setting, MMBench [ 19 ] adds an LLM choice-extractor and circular evaluation
inside a new benchmark. A stronger response is to abandon the format outright: Chandak et al. [7] show that free-form answer matching , graded against a reference by a
capable model, reaches human-level agreement where multiple choice does not, and argue evaluation should
move off discriminative MCQ. That is a prescription for the benchmarks of the future; ours is a diagnosis
of the ones in use today. These make the parser better, the protocol uniform, the benchmark harder, or the
format different, but none audits, for existing multimodal benchmarks, what the scorer does when the
parser fails . We target exactly that residual: the parse-failure fallback, measured against what
the model actually answered.

A separate line argues multimodal LLMs should be allowed to abstain and that benchmarks mismeasure when they force
a choice [ 24 ] . We share the premise but apply it to the grader : the parse-failure fallback
is a forced choice imposed by the grading code, independent of whether the model tried to abstain.

blocks.en:
A recurring genre re-examines a trusted evaluation practice and finds it unreliable: GAN metrics under
equal compute budgets [ 22 ] , deep metric-learning gains under fair comparison [ 26 ] . The genre is now active for LLM and multimodal evaluation and well
represented at datasets-and-benchmarks venues: judge reliability [ 38 ] , benchmark
robustness and format noise [ 31 ] , multimodal harness reality-checks [ 35 ] ,
lexical matching that underestimates generative models against human
judgment [ 17 ] , grading logic that over-credits agents [ 39 ] , and,
closest to us in modality, dataset validity for LVLMs [ 8 ] (visual necessity and
leakage). We are the reality-check for the scoring rule of multimodal-LLM multiple-choice
evaluation. Unlike a general reproduction, we hold each benchmark’s own official parser fixed and change
only the parse-failure fallback, which attributes the measured gap to the scoring rule alone.

Let a multiple-choice item have k k options and gold answer g g ; the model emits free text r r . A scoring
rule is a function s ⁡ ( r ) → { 1 , … , k } ∪ { ⊥ } s(r)\to\{1,\dots,k\}\cup\{\bot\} , where ⊥ \bot means abstain (scored wrong). The rule

parser fails. Both embed unreported decisions: where the parser looks and how it breaks ties among
several candidate letters, and what the scorer does when it finds nothing. Our headline measurements
isolate the fallback, which is where these benchmarks differ most and which is almost never justified or
reported; Sec. 5.3 shows the parser side is not inert either, and that it is the side the
field’s move to reasoning models activates. their own way, and which rule is least wrong is model-dependent.

blocks.en:
We use five current open vision-language models that each run 4-bit on a single 16 GB GPU:
Gemma-4-E4B [ 10 ] , Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 3 ] , Qwen3-VL-8B [ 4 ] ,
Pixtral-12B [ 1 ] , and Llama-3.2-11B-Vision [ 11 ] . For each benchmark we clone the
official repository at a pinned commit and call its released scoring function on our models’ outputs; we
do not reimplement the scorer. Non-compliance is not an artifact of under-specified prompting: MMAD’s
released prompt already ends “Answer with the option’s letter from the given choices directly,” and
Pixtral still fails to emit a letter on 489 / 1,670 489/1{,}670 items ( 29 % 29\% ), once replying “Here’s the option’s
letter from the choices directly.” We generate every response with greedy decoding (temperature 0 0 ),
so the stored outputs are deterministic and carry no sampling variance; this is what licenses our
“same outputs, every rule” design, since all rule differences are then attributable to the scorer
alone. Models are loaded in 4-bit (bitsandbytes NF4, bfloat16 compute) with a generation budget
of 16 16 tokens on the letter-answer benchmarks and up to 768 768 on the chain-of-thought ones. ScienceQA is
the one benchmark whose non-compliance is a format mismatch rather than a failure to answer
(Sec. 5.3 ), so we treat its magnitude as a code-presence
finding only (Sec. 3 ). Elsewhere non-compliance is a property of the models, not the budget:
quadrupling it to 64 64 tokens (Tab. 2 ) leaves MMAD non-compliance nearly flat and the snap
artifact large, because these models describe the image or answer in words rather than emit a letter. As
a validity check we score our stored outputs twice, once with MMAD’s own released harness
( caculate_accuracy_mmad ) and once with our wrapper, and their per-item verdicts agree to
four decimals on four of five models (its printed headline further macro-averages the normal/anomaly
split; we report plain accuracy). The fifth, Pixtral, differs by 0.2 0.2 points because the harness keeps
the last regex match where our wrapper keeps the first: immaterial here, since only Pixtral ever
emits two option letters ( 19 19 of 8,350 8{,}350 responses) and the artifact is identical under both
conventions, but the same unreported choice that decides 9.5 9.5 points on a reasoning model
(Sec. 5.3 ).

To anchor the rules to ground truth we adjudicate what the model actually answered. For each item we
build a blinded record containing only the question, the options, and the model’s full response;
the gold answer and every rule’s verdict are withheld. A reader assigns one label: a letter (the model
committed to that option, by letter or by stating its text), none (it never committed: it
described, hedged, refused, or ran out), or multiple (contradictory). The join from saved
responses to questions is verified by matching the gold sequence (it aborts on mismatch).

blocks.en:
Anchored to the human label ( κ = 0.956 \kappa=0.956 , Sec. 4 ), each rule fails differently. On the 110 110 non-compliant MMAD items, the model committed to an option only 23 % 23\% of the time, yet the
snap scored 72 % 72\% “correct”: it credits answers the model never gave. Abstention has the opposite
failure: on the 17 % 17\% of those items where the model did state the gold answer in words (“No.”), the
letter-only rule marks it wrong. Likelihood scoring fails a third way (Sec. 5.3 ). There is
no neutral default: the snap over-credits, abstention under-credits, and the gap between them on MMAD
( 0.21 0.21 ) is a gap between two flawed rules, not a measurement of the model. The 22 22 -point figure needs
no adjudication: it is exact on all 1,670 1{,}670 items; adjudication supports only the stronger claim that
neither rule recovers what the model said. The two rules also span the
scores a reporting policy can produce on the full set: [ 0.444 , 0.656 ] [0.444,0.656] for Pixtral, [ 0.522 , 0.741 ] [0.522,0.741] for
Llama. We report that as a policy-sensitivity interval, not a bound on adjudicated accuracy: the snap
under-credits even on MMAD (Table 5 ), the lower end assumes a parsed letter is the committed answer, which Sec. 5.3 (v) shows can fail, and on PMC-VQA the ordering
inverts.

Five further results show no rule is a safe default. (i) The same scorer adds 22 22 points to one model and removes 19 19 from another (Fig. 3 ) . PMC-VQA’s matcher is unconditional (it runs on every response), so besides filling parse failures it can override an
answer the parser already read. Separating the two on identical outputs, the fallback alone adds + 0.097 +0.097 to Pixtral and + 0.020 +0.020 to Llama, while the override subtracts 0.210 0.210 from Llama, mapping onto a
different option the answer its own parser reads as gold on 153 / 600 153/600 items ( 25.5 % 25.5\% of the
benchmark). The aggregate − 0.190 -0.190 is the sum, and the larger term is not the fallback, a distinction
our other benchmarks never force, because their matchers run only when the parser fails. Anchored to the
human label the fallback is bidirectional too. A 60 60 -item audit (judge–human κ = 0.84 \kappa=0.84 , 0.95 0.95 on the
commit-vs-no-commit split this turns on) confirms a real per-item effect: the snap under-credits Llama on 31 % 31\% of items, marking wrong medical answers it actually gave, while over-crediting Pixtral on 10 % 10\% ; the split is unchanged whether unaudited items anchor to the human or the judge ( 0.29 → 0.31 0.29{\to}0.31 ). “Unreliable,” not
“optimistic.” Because the sign of the error flips with the model’s verbosity and the dataset’s option
format, the grader acts as a confound : it injects variance tied to response length rather than
capability, so one unexamined grade measures neither cleanly. A weak probe agrees: on items where a human found no single
committed option, the model’s own option likelihood prefers gold at chance for Pixtral ( 26 / 52 26/52 )
but above chance for Llama ( 24 / 34 24/34 , two-sided p = 0.024 p{=}0.024 ), so even the character of the snap’s unearned
credit is model-dependent; the single-token logit is itself token-prior biased [ 13 , 30 ] (ii), so we do not read
this as a capability claim. (ii) The principled rule can be the most wrong: 0.403 0.403 against the snap’s 0.565 0.565 . Parse-free likelihood is not a clean ground
truth: on OmniMedVQA, Llama’s option-letter logit collapses onto the token “A” on 459 / 600 459/600 items while
gold is “A” only 29 % 29\% of the time, giving accuracy 0.403 0.403 , below the snap’s 0.565 0.565 . Any
single rule, including the principled one, can be the most wrong. (iii) An extraction buffer defuses the idiom: + 10 +10 points collapses to + 0.9 +0.9 . MathVista runs an LLM extraction step before the same
no-threshold snap; scoring the snap on raw responses yields a spurious + 10 +10 -point artifact, but the
faithful pipeline (extraction first, reproduced with a local model) collapses it to + 0.9 +0.9 points,
evidence that the fix is a competent parse, not a different fallback. (iv) One character of unreported regex is worth 29.5 29.5 points. ScienceQA is the purest case, and not for the reason we
first assumed: its released regex demands the literal The answer is X. , and the models answer The answer is (X). instead. Of Llama’s 507 507 parse failures, 460 460 contain that
parenthesised form and none is truncated (median response 110 110 characters). The scorer therefore
discards answers that are present and correct, and randomly fabricates in their place: accepting both
spellings (abstaining on the residual failures) raises Llama from 0.448 0.448 to 0.743 0.743 on identical
stored outputs ( ≈ 0.80 {\approx}0.80 keeping that fallback instead). A single character of
unreported regex is worth 29.5 29.5 points to one model, which is the thesis of this paper in its least
ambiguous form. (v) Non-compliance 0.000 0.000 , and the grade still moves 9.5 9.5 points. Every scorer we audit applies its
parser to the entire response: harmless when models emitted two characters, not once they
reason first. On MMAD, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking is fully format-compliant: non-compliance 0.000 0.000 , the
parse-failure fallback fires zero times, the artifact this paper measures is exactly 0 0 , and it
closes its </think> block within budget on 99.8 % 99.8\% of 1,670 1{,}670 items. Yet its trace restates
MMAD’s option list before answering, so which regex match the scorer keeps now decides the grade.
MMAD’s eleven majority harnesses keep the last and recover the model’s stated answer on 1666 / 1666 1666/1666 items; the two that keep the first disagree with it on 15.9 % 15.9\% and score
identical outputs at 0.689 0.689 rather than 0.784 0.784 , a 9.5 9.5 -point gap (category-clustered 95 % 95\% CI [ 6.4 , 13.1 ] [6.4,13.1] , 15 15 MVTec [ 5 ] categories). The benchmark ships both numbers and reports neither choice. This
is not a capability claim: correctly scored, the reasoning model ( 0.784 0.784 ) still trails its instruction-tuned
sibling ( 0.837 0.837 ) on these items. It is the sharper form of our recommendation: a non-compliance rate of 0 0 certifies that nothing was fabricated, not that the grade is safe, a pattern Jo et al. [16] document for text LLMs and we find in shipped multimodal scoring code. MathVision [ 29 ] makes
the same point from the opposite direction, abstaining rather than snapping at the highest
non-compliance we measure (Tab. 4 ): what converts rambling into a corrupted score is the
fallback, not the difficulty.

Holding each benchmark’s parser fixed and varying only the fallback, we find no robust leaderboard
reordering: the strongest model stays top-ranked, and a top-1 change on MMMU under abstention is not
significant at our sample size ( p = 0.58 p\!=\!0.58 ). Where the released parser is itself the variable the
picture differs: accepting ScienceQA’s near-miss format moves Llama from last to fourth, which is one
reason we report ScienceQA as a code-presence finding rather than folding it into the headline. The
contribution is the unreliability of the grade, not a corrected ranking: stable ranks are the weaker
guarantee, and the same ordering sits on a 21 21 -point spread in the number practitioners deploy by and
later papers must match.
Nor does a shared harness dissolve it: VLMEvalKit ships the same random fallback (Sec. 1 ),
and the thirteen harnesses inside MMAD alone disagree with each other by 9.5 9.5 points (item v).

blocks.en: 6 Recommendation
blocks.zh: 6 建议

blocks.en:
No single scoring rule reflects what a model knew or said, so a benchmark should not hide its choice of
rule inside a scoring script and report one number. We recommend three low-cost practices.
blocks.zh:
没有任何单一的评分规则能反映一个模型所知道或所说的话,因此基准不应掩盖其选择
规则在评分脚本中并报告一个数字。 我们建议采取三种低成本做法。

blocks.en:
1. Report the non-compliance rate (the fraction of outputs on which the parse-failure
fallback fires) alongside accuracy. It is one number, and it is the single statistic that exposes how
much of a score the grader manufactured; when it is large, the headline accuracy is not comparable
across papers. It is necessary but not sufficient, and reasoning models are where the difference
starts to matter: a model can be perfectly compliant (non-compliance 0 0 , the fallback never
firing) while its grade still turns on where in the response the parser looks
(Sec. 5.3 ). Report the rate, and state the parser’s scope and tie-break alongside it. 2. Report at least two rules. Publish accuracy under both an abstaining rule (crediting
only parseable letters) and the closest-option snap, rather than a single grade under either alone.
On MMAD, where adjudication shows the snap rarely under-credits, the spread approximates the range of
defensible scores; on PMC-VQA it inverts, the snap scoring Llama below the abstaining rule. Unconditionally, the spread is the rule-sensitivity a single
number hides, and a spread that inverts is itself the warning. Likelihood scoring is a useful parse-free cross-check, not a safe
default: it too can be the most-wrong rule (Sec. 5.3 ). 3. Adjudicate when it matters. Our blinded human-plus-LLM-judge protocol ( κ = 0.956 \kappa=0.956 )
recovers what the model actually answered for roughly one person-day per benchmark, and the certified
judge can then label the full non-compliant set automatically, at no further human cost. We release the adjudication corpus : one stored generation per item for all eight benchmarks and five models, 130 130 blinded MMAD adjudications ( 40 40 dual-annotated by a reader naive to the hypothesis, κ HH = 0.91 \kappa_{\mathrm{HH}}=0.91 ), 60 60 blinded PMC-VQA adjudications, and the certified judge’s labels on the
audited items, with the manifest builder, blinded MCQ tool, judge, and analysis code, under
permissive licenses (MIT / CC-BY-4.0), with a datasheet and one-command containerized reproduction, so
any benchmark author can audit what their grader credits.

blocks.en: 8 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8 结论

blocks.en:
A benchmark score is read as a measurement of the model. But when a model rambles, as the locally
deployable models these benchmarks target routinely do, part of that score is manufactured by a grading
choice no paper wrote down. Scores are therefore not comparable across papers that chose differently,
and the remedy is nearly free: state the rule, report how often it fires, publish more than one number. We give a certified procedure for checking what a grader credits, and hope
the next benchmark affords the last lines of its scoring code the scrutiny it affords its data: the
dataset is not the only thing worth reviewing.
